ch15.title: Let Us Go and Die with Him
ch15.b002: February nights in Philadelphia were noisier than the days. In the courtyard where the believers were lodged, the lamps burned late, and now and then sheep bleated in the valley outside the walls. It was Sunday, February 26, A.D. 30. The evening council had ended, and the Master was saying good night to the apostles. John Zebedee stood in the doorway, waiting for his brother James to pull on his cloak. Just then the courtyard gate was flung open and a man came in, out of breath from a long run. He was a runner from Bethany, and he brought word from Martha and Mary. The one the Master loved, the message said, was very sick.
ch15.b003: As soon as John heard it, he saw Lazarus’s face. The wide olive orchards at Bethany, the vineyards on the hillside, the house that had taken in the Master and the twelve every time they went up to Jerusalem. Lazarus was a man who did not laugh much, but the hand that opened his door was always generous. Martha was forever hurrying between the kitchen and the yard; Mary sat at the Master’s feet and listened. John knew better than anyone how dear those three were to the Master. He had long acted for Jesus in the affairs of his family, and he had watched from close by how the Master, homeless and always on the road, still held in his heart the people he loved.
ch15.b004: But the Master did not answer at once. The courtyard grew quiet. He stood with his head bowed a little, and to John the posture was familiar. Now and then the Master would stop like that, like a man in conversation with something beyond himself, and for those few moments no one could speak to him. At last he raised his head and, with the apostles listening, spoke to the runner. This sickness, he said, was really not to the death. The runner was not to doubt that it could be used to glorify God and exalt the Son.
ch15.b005: The runner took the answer and left. John felt his heart settle. If the Master said so, it was so. That night he lay beside his brother looking up into the dark and thought that in the morning they would turn back toward Pella. For these weeks of touring Perea there had been only ten of them with the Master. Peter and Andrew had once again stayed behind at the Pella camp to teach the crowds gathered there. John found it a little funny how used he was getting to evenings without Peter’s noise.
ch15.b007: The next morning the Master said nothing about leaving. Nor the morning after that. He met people with Abner, asked about the synagogue, and spent the day as he always did. The apostles got through those two days each in his own way.
ch15.b008: Thomas was the manager of their itinerary. When the company would move and where, which village they would sleep in, how the water and the roads and the weather fitted together: that was his work. By his reckoning they ought to have started back to Pella on Monday. He erased that date in his head and wrote it in again more than once. The Master said nothing. Thomas did not ask. But he set the news from Bethany beside the Master’s silence and looked at the two together for a long time. A dear friend was sick, and the Master was not going. That meant he had a reason for not going. And whatever the reason, every picture that rose in Thomas’s mind was a dark one. Bethany was less than an hour’s walk from Jerusalem. A few weeks earlier, in that city, the leaders had sought the Master’s life and the people had picked up stones.
ch15.b009: During those two days Matthew Levi sat several times beside Judas Iscariot while Judas went over the accounts. The believers at Philadelphia had been generous, and for once the apostolic purse was heavy. Judas stacked the coins and said little. Then once, as if to himself, he murmured that Bethany was right on Jerusalem’s doorstep. Matthew caught something at the end of the words that was less fear than calculation, as if Judas were weighing something. Judas knew Jerusalem. He was the only one of the twelve who had grown up in Judea, and he knew in his bones what the Sadducean families of that city were like. Matthew found that fact sticking in his mind. But he could not put into words what it was that bothered him.
ch15.b010: John watched the Master’s face through both days. There was no shadow of worry on it. That troubled John more than worry would have. The Master loved Lazarus; there was no doubting that. And yet he stayed. John spent two nights unable to fit those two things together. In later years he would think about those two days often: that there are times when the one who loves stays where he is while the one he loves is waiting. But the John of those days was not yet old enough to understand it.
ch15.b012: Early on Wednesday morning the Master called the apostles and told them to get ready at once; they were going into Judea again.
ch15.b013: The apostles looked at one another. Then they drew off by themselves to talk it over. It was James Zebedee who led the discussion. With Peter and Andrew absent, the task fell to him naturally. The talk was short. The ten were of one mind. To let the Master go into Judea now would be nothing but folly.
ch15.b014: They came back as one man, and James spoke for them all. A few weeks ago, when he was in Jerusalem, the leaders had sought his death and the people had wanted to stone him. He had already given those men their chance to receive the truth. They would not let him go into Judea again. James’s voice was louder than usual. He was a man who talked a great deal only when he was angry, and his anger now was not at the Master but at the men who wanted him dead.
ch15.b015: The Master looked round at them. Were there not twelve hours in the day, he asked, in which work could safely be done? A man who walked by day did not stumble, because he had light; a man who walked by night was apt to stumble. As long as his own day lasted, he was not afraid to enter Judea. He wanted to do one more mighty work for those people, to give them one more chance to believe, even on their own terms. And besides, he added, their friend Lazarus had fallen asleep, and he was going to wake him.
ch15.b016: One of them said, with relief, that if Lazarus had fallen asleep he would surely recover. John had heard it the same way. Sleep meant the fever had broken. Then the Master told them plainly. Lazarus was dead. And for their sakes he was glad he had not been there, so that they would have a new reason to believe in him, and so that what they were about to see would strengthen them all for the day when he would leave them and go to the Father.
ch15.b017: Dead. The word reached John late. He thought of the runner on Sunday night, of the words about a sickness that was not to the death. He set the two sayings side by side and lost his way between them.
ch15.b019: They could not dissuade him. The Master’s face was already set on the road ahead. A heavy silence fell on the apostles. Some of them were plainly reluctant even to go with him. No one said so, but no one moved to pack, as if their feet had grown into the ground.
ch15.b020: Thomas stood in the middle of that silence. A few minutes earlier, in the council, he had argued against the journey more firmly than anyone. He always did. If he thought a course reckless, he fought it to the end, pointing out each danger in turn. And the conclusion he had reached now was perfectly clear. To go to Bethany was to go to Jerusalem, and to go to Jerusalem was to go and die. He did not doubt it. He was a man of many doubts, but here there was nothing to doubt.
ch15.b021: For a moment he thought of his house at Tarichea. His wife and four children. When he had left to become an apostle, his wife had looked less sorry than relieved, thinking her gloomy husband would be away from home most of the time. Thomas did not blame her. He was not an easy man to live with. If he died at Bethany, she would weep, but she would not weep long. The thought did not hurt him. Oddly, it made him lighter. What he held on to now was not that house but this company. Ever since he lost his twin sister when he was nine, he had believed that the world would sooner or later take away whatever was most precious. Now the world was reaching out to take something again. This time, Thomas thought, he would not stand alone in the place of the one who loses.
ch15.b022: And something else was rising in him. He had been a stone mason. Anyone who works with stone knows that once the decision is made to lay a foundation, you stop debating. You lift the stone. When he opposed a thing he opposed it to the end, but to back away once the decision had been made was not how a working man did things. And the one who had decided this time was not a vote of ten men. It was the Master.
ch15.b023: Thomas looked round at his companions. The twins with their heads down, Simon Zelotes with his jaw clenched, Philip drumming his fingers on his knee, Nathaniel gone pale, Judas Iscariot gazing at something far off, and the sons of Zebedee with set faces. He drew a deep breath.
ch15.b024: “We’ve told the Master everything we’re afraid of. And still he’s made up his mind to go to Bethany. I think this is the end. They’ll kill him, as sure as anything.”
ch15.b025: He stopped for a moment. No one breathed.
ch15.b026: “But if that’s what the Master has chosen, then let’s act like men with some courage. Come on. Let’s go too, and die with him.”
ch15.b027: When he had finished, Thomas was surprised to find that his voice had not shaken at all. He was afraid. The fear was still there. But something solid had been set down on top of it: that they would be with the Master. With that, even a road to death was a road.
ch15.b028: The twins got up first, almost together, and almost together walked over to their bundles. Simon Zelotes gave a short laugh, the face of a man who had never heard talk like that even among the Zealots. Philip got up and began counting out provisions. Nathaniel gripped Thomas’s shoulder once and let go.
ch15.b029: Matthew was the last to rise, and he looked at Thomas a long time as he did. This man always saw the darkest side first. His companions sometimes found him tiresome for it. Yet today those dark eyes had been the first to open the way. The man who saw the danger most clearly was the first to walk into it. For the first time Matthew understood clearly that this was what courage was. That day he thought that in anything needing steady courage, Thomas was the mainstay of the twelve, and he never had reason to change his mind.
ch15.b030: Judas Iscariot, packing, wound the strings of the purse round twice. He had nodded at Thomas’s words, but his own reckoning was running somewhere else. Going to die? No. The Master meant to do something on Jerusalem’s doorstep. He had said he would give them a chance to believe, even on their own terms. Then at last, Judas thought. At last he means to stop hiding that power and show it. His step grew a little lighter.
ch15.b032: They left Philadelphia on Wednesday morning. On the road down to the Jordan nearly fifty people followed them, friends among them and enemies too, come to watch the Master. At noon they stopped by the road to eat, and the Master spoke to the apostles and the company about the terms of salvation.
ch15.b033: Matthew listened with a piece of dry bread in his hand. The Master said that salvation was a free gift the Father gave to all who had the faith to receive sonship in his family. There was nothing a man could do to earn it; acts of self-righteousness could not buy God’s favor. Then he told a story. Two men went up to the temple to pray, he said, one a Pharisee and the other a publican, a tax collector.
ch15.b034: A publican. Matthew put down the bread. In the Master’s story the Pharisee stood and thanked God that he was not like other men, and especially not like that publican. He fasted, he said, and he paid his tithes. But the publican stood far off, would not even lift his eyes to heaven, beat his breast, and asked only that God be merciful to him, a sinner. It was the publican, the Master said, who went home with God’s approval. Whoever exalted himself would be humbled, and whoever humbled himself would be exalted.
ch15.b035: Matthew could not raise his eyes. He remembered his days in the customs house at Capernaum. He had never beaten his breast. He had only felt something heavy settle in him every evening as he closed the books. The publican in the story claimed nothing for himself. And suddenly Matthew wondered whether his own wish, that the Master would notice how he had been quietly filling the apostles’ purse, was perhaps not so far from the Pharisee’s prayer. The thought shamed him, and at the same time it made him strangely light. He was a man who did not need to bring anything. The publican had gone empty-handed, and so he had received.
ch15.b036: Thomas, sitting beside him, said quietly:
ch15.b037: “Your face looks easier in that story than anyone else’s.”
ch15.b038: Matthew did not answer; he picked up his bread again. That night in Jericho some Pharisees tried to trap the Master into an argument about marriage and divorce, but he slipped past the net and only spoke of marriage as the highest of human relationships.
ch15.b039: The next morning, before breakfast, scores of Jericho mothers came to the house where the Master was staying, carrying their children in their arms and leading them by the hand. His words the evening before about marriage and the blessedness of children had spread through the whole town. The apostles went out and tried to send them away. They had a long way to go, and they had to reach Bethany that day. When the mothers would not leave, the apostles raised their voices. John was among them, standing with his arms spread in front of the women who blocked the way.
ch15.b040: Then the Master came out. On his face was an indignation John had seldom seen. He reproved the apostles. They were not to stop the children from coming to him, he said; the kingdom of heaven belonged to such as these. Whoever did not receive the kingdom like a little child would hardly grow up in it to full spiritual stature. And the Master took the children one by one and laid his hands on them.
ch15.b041: Slowly John lowered his arms. Once before he had stood in the way of strangers who were teaching in the Master’s name. Then too he had believed he was doing right. He believed it now. He had been guarding the Master, saving his time. But the Master had never asked to be guarded. John watched the Master’s back as he laid his hands on the children and thought about whom it was he had always been standing in front of. It was a small thorn lodged in his heart that morning, and it stayed there a long time.
ch15.b043: The road up from Jericho to Bethany was steep. It wound back and forth between rocky slopes, and as the sun climbed the stones grew hot. Nathaniel walked most of the way at the Master’s side. Their talk, which had started with children, had somehow turned to angels. Nathaniel asked what they should teach people about the heavenly ministers, seeing that the high priest was a Sadducee and the Sadducees did not believe in angels, and the Master answered him at length as they walked. John, a few steps behind, listening, found it remarkable that on the road up into a land of death the Master could speak so calmly about the things of heaven.
ch15.b044: As they came over the brow of the hill, they saw a woman running toward them along the road. It was Martha. It was a little after noon. Martha fell at the Master’s feet and cried out that if he had been there, her brother would not have died.
ch15.b045: John listened for reproach in her voice and did not find it. It was not an accusing cry but a breaking one. Martha did not question anything after it. The Master bent and lifted her to her feet. Only have faith, he told her, and her brother would rise again. Martha answered that she knew he would rise in the resurrection at the last day, and that even now she believed God would give him whatever he asked.
ch15.b046: The Master looked straight into her eyes and said that he was the resurrection and the life. Whoever believed in him would live, even though he died, and whoever lived and believed in him would never really die. Did she believe this? Martha answered that she had long believed he was the Deliverer, the Son of the living God.
ch15.b047: John held his breath as he listened. The resurrection and the life. He laid the words away somewhere deep within him. When he was a very old man he would still remember them, together with the sunlight on that hill and Martha’s wet face.
ch15.b048: When the Master asked for Mary, Martha went into the house and whispered to her sister. The house was full of mourners, and among them were not a few of the Master’s enemies from Jerusalem. Martha knew it, and that was why she had come out alone to meet him. But when Mary got up quickly and went out, the mourners thought she was going to weep at the tomb and crowded out after her. When Mary saw the Master, she fell at his feet and said the same words her sister had said.
ch15.b049: The Master saw the two sisters weeping, and the people who had come with them weeping, and his soul was deeply moved. John saw it. What crossed the Master’s face was not grief alone. There was something there for those who mourned only outwardly, mixed in among the sincere ones: men who wanted him dead in their hearts and wept loudly in front of a grave. John knew how much the Master disliked that kind of show.
ch15.b050: The Master asked where they had laid him. Martha said, Come and see. And as he walked in silence behind the two sisters, the Master wept.
ch15.b051: John, walking behind, saw the tears. He had never seen the Master weep before. He knew this man had said he was coming to wake Lazarus. And still he wept. John could not see why anyone would weep over a man he was about to raise. He only knew the tears were not false. Perhaps the Master wept for the two women at the tomb. Perhaps for those who wept only on the outside. Perhaps for what Lazarus would have to suffer once he was brought back. John could not tie all the reasons into one. But that day he saw for the first time how fully human was the one he followed. And he saw that it made him not one bit smaller.
ch15.b052: One of the friendly Jews walking behind murmured that they should look how he had loved him. Could not the man who had opened the blind man’s eyes have kept this one from dying? Elsewhere there were sneers. If he cared so much for the man, why had he taken so long to come? What was the use of healing strangers in Galilee if he could not save those he loved?
ch15.b054: The tomb was a small cave at the far end of the garden, in a ledge of rock that rose some thirty feet above the garden floor. A large stone closed its entrance. It had been rolled into place that very morning. About forty-five people gathered in front of it. Early spring sunlight lay white on the rock, and the leaves of the garden olives flashed silver when the wind turned them. It was about half past two on Thursday afternoon.
ch15.b055: The Master told them to take away the stone.
ch15.b056: Martha hesitated. Her brother had been dead four days, she said; by now the body would have begun to decay. Mary said nothing. The Master asked whether he had not told them at the first that this sickness was not to the death. Had he not come to keep his promise? Had he not said that if they would only believe, they would see the glory of God? Why did they doubt? How long before they would believe and obey?
ch15.b057: The apostles went to the stone. Some of the neighbors willingly lent a hand. Thomas set his palm against its edge. Under his hand he felt the cold, rough grain of the limestone. He had lifted and moved and dressed countless stones like this one. Gauging weight with his hands was a habit of many years. But with this stone it seemed he was measuring something other than weight. What was behind it. Four days of death. He clenched his teeth and drove his shoulder in. The stone ground across the floor and rolled. Cool, damp air from the cave touched his face.
ch15.b058: In the dim interior, in the lower niche on the right, they could just make out a shape wrapped in linen. Someone caught his breath. Matthew stepped half a pace back. In his customs-house days he had seen death more than once. But he had never opened the mouth of a tomb and looked inside. Judas Iscariot, in the crowd, was craning his neck. His eyes were not on the cave. They were on the Master.
ch15.b059: The Master lifted his eyes and thanked his Father. He was thankful, he said, that the Father had heard and granted his request. He knew the Father always heard him, but he spoke aloud like this for the sake of the people standing there, so that they would believe the Father had sent him and know that the Father was working with him in what they were about to do.
ch15.b060: Then he cried out in a loud voice:
ch15.b062: No one moved. Even the wind seemed to stop. Thomas was counting his breaths; counting things was a habit of his. One. Two. He reached twelve. And then the shape in the cave moved. The body bound in linen sat up on the edge of the stone shelf. Its face was covered with a cloth. And then the body stood.
ch15.b063: The Master told them to loose him and let him go.
ch15.b064: What came next happened all at once. People cried out and scattered. Mourners with faces gone white with fright fled across the garden to the house. Some lingered, but many hurried away to their homes. Before the tomb there remained only the apostles, with Martha and Mary.
ch15.b065: John stayed where he was. He felt his legs trembling, but he did not run. Matthew stayed too. From the place half a step back where he had stopped, he went no further. The twins were holding each other by the arm. Simon Zelotes stood with his mouth open. Something was blazing in his face. With that, with that power, anything could be done. The thought showed plainly in his eyes.
ch15.b066: Lazarus walked out of the tomb and greeted the Master and the apostles. Then he asked what these grave cloths meant and why he had woken up in the garden. While the Master and the apostles stepped to one side, Martha explained to her brother that he had died on Sunday and been buried, and that today, Thursday, he had been brought back to life. Lazarus knew nothing of those four days. To him it was only that he had fallen asleep and woken.
ch15.b067: Lazarus came and knelt with his two sisters at the Master’s feet and gave thanks to God. The Master took him by the hand and lifted him up. What had happened to him, he said, would also happen to all who believed this gospel, except that they would rise in a more glorious form. He would be a living witness to the truth that the Master was the resurrection and the life. And now, he said, let them all go into the house and eat, for their bodies needed it.
ch15.b068: Walking back to the house, Thomas looked down at his palm. It was white with stone dust. He did not brush it off. It was only yesterday morning that he had said, Let us go and die with him. He had come to see death, and he had seen life. How the two could be joined in a single day he could not tell. But for the first time Thomas gladly accepted that his darkest reckoning had been wrong.
ch15.b069: Judas Iscariot walked at the back. His heart was beating fast. Now, he thought. When Jerusalem hears of this, no one will be able to stop him. Now he cannot hide that power any longer. The thought kept him warm all that evening.
ch15.b071: By noon the next day the story had spread all over Jerusalem. Scores of people came out to Bethany to look at Lazarus and talk with him. And that Friday afternoon the Sanhedrin met. A certain Pharisee proposed that Jesus be put to death at once, without a trial, and fourteen members of the council resigned on the spot. At that same meeting Caiaphas the high priest first spoke the old saying that it was better for one man to die than for the community to perish.
ch15.b072: The news reached Bethpage that evening, where the Master was resting over the Sabbath with friends. The apostles’ faces went hard when they heard it, but the Master was not disturbed in the least. Matthew could not understand that calm. Yet, oddly, it steadied him. That night he climbed onto a low roof in Bethpage and looked toward Jerusalem. Beyond the Mount of Olives the city’s lights spread faintly. Somewhere under those lights men were calculating the Master’s death. From his years at the customs table, Matthew knew well how the faces of calculating men hardened. Once they had settled a thing in figures, they did not easily change it. He climbed down and lay among his sleeping companions. He could hear the even breathing of the twins. Matthew lay listening to it with his eyes open for a long time.
ch15.b073: Early on Sunday morning they gathered at Lazarus’s house as arranged, took leave of the Bethany family, and set out secretly. They were going back to Pella. No crowd followed them, and for the first time in a long while the ten walked alone around the Master.
ch15.b074: On the road the apostles asked him many things. He answered every question freely except those about the details of raising the dead. The thing they kept coming back to, all that day, was the answer to prayer. At Philadelphia the Master had said that this sickness was not to the death. And yet Lazarus had really died. How were the two to be fitted together?
ch15.b075: “The way I count it, Lazarus was already dead before the runner ever reached Philadelphia,” said Philip, ticking it off on his fingers.
ch15.b076: “Then did the Master know from the beginning?”
ch15.b077: No one could answer. In reply to their questions the Master told them that when a prayer seems to go unanswered, the delay often means a better answer. No sincere prayer is refused, he said, except when the higher view of the spiritual world has prepared a better answer, one that meets what a man’s spirit asked for rather than what his mind alone asked for. And prayer must be born of the spirit and nourished by faith; true faith had already given the hearers of prayer the full right to answer it in their own wisdom and love.
ch15.b078: John walked on, turning the words over. A delayed answer. He thought of the two days at Philadelphia. Then he had not understood why the one who loved should stay where he was. He did not fully understand it even now. But he understood a little that the doubts he had held in those two days had not been aimed at the Master but at his own narrow reckoning. His brother James walked silently beside him. John nudged his arm once. James looked round, but John said nothing.
ch15.b079: Thomas was out in front, setting the route. The itinerary was back in his hands. He counted the days to Pella, and for the first time in a long while the counting felt light. The Master had said he wanted to make them strong for the day when he would go to the Father. Thomas had made a point of not hearing that part. The day when he would go to the Father. That, at least, he did not want to put into his reckoning yet.
ch15.b080: Late on Monday evening, March 6, they reached the Pella camp. The news of Lazarus had arrived two days ahead of them. The whole camp was buzzing, and the torches burned late. Peter came running through the crowd. His voice rang out loudly in the dark, asking them to tell him everything that had happened. Andrew came behind him slowly and looked at the faces of the ten one by one. They were all safe. He made sure of that much, and nodded.
ch15.b081: That night the apostles sat around the fire and told what had happened at Bethany. Peter asked the most questions and was the most amazed. The twins imitated the sound of the stone rolling. Matthew was about to bring up the story of the Pharisee and the publican, then let it go. He wanted to keep that story to himself a while longer.
ch15.b082: As Andrew listened, he watched Judas Iscariot. By the fire Judas’s face was brighter than anyone’s. When he told what he had seen at the tomb there was heat in his voice. It was joy. And yet Andrew felt that this joy was somehow different in grain from the joy of the others. The others were glad that Lazarus had been brought back to life. Judas seemed glad that something was about to begin. Andrew did not know what to call the difference. And so, once again, he said nothing.
ch15.b083: Thomas sat on a rock a little way from the fire. He rubbed his palms together. The stone dust had all fallen away somewhere on the road. He remembered saying, Let us go and die with him. Those words, Thomas dimly felt, had not yet been fully spent. One day the time would come when they were truly needed. Whether he would be able to say them again that day, he could not tell. But that day had not yet come. Tonight the fires of Pella were warm, and the Master was resting in his tent.
ch15.b085: The course of events follows Papers 167 and 168: during the Perean tour Peter and Andrew remained at Pella while ten apostles went with Jesus (167:0.1); the arrival at Philadelphia (167:0.3); the Bethany runner’s arrival late on Sunday night, February 26, and Jesus’ answer, the two further days at Philadelphia, the Wednesday-morning call to go into Judea and the apostles’ objection led by James, the twelve hours of the day and Lazarus fallen asleep, and Thomas rallying his fellows when some were loath to go (167:4.1–4.7); the company of almost fifty, the parable of the Pharisee and the publican, and the divorce question at Jericho (167:5.1–5.3); Jesus reproving the apostles who sent the children away (167:6.1–6.2); Nathaniel’s talk with Jesus about angels and Martha’s coming out to meet him (167:7.1–7.7); the words with Martha and Mary, Jesus’ tears, the tomb and the forty-five onlookers, the apostles rolling away the stone, the prayer and the raising of Lazarus after twelve seconds, the flight of the onlookers, and Lazarus’s questions and thanksgiving (168:0.1–2.9); the Friday session of the Sanhedrin and Caiaphas’s adage, the Sabbath at Bethpage, and the secret departure early on Sunday (168:2.10–3.7); the conversations on the road about the answering of prayer (168:4.1–4.13); and the arrival at Pella on March 6, with the news arriving two days before (169:0.1–0.2).
ch15.b086: Character details come from Paper 139: Thomas opposing a plan in council but being the first to move once it was decided, and rallying the others with “let’s go and die with him” (139:8.8, 167:4.7); his work as manager of the itinerary, his trade as carpenter and stone mason, his family at Tarichea and the loss of his twin sister (139:8.2, 8.3, 8.5, 8.10); Matthew secretly making up the apostolic funds and wishing Jesus knew of it (139:7.8–7.9); John acting for Jesus in his family affairs and forbidding strangers to teach (139:4.1, 4.8); Judas as the only Judean and his belief that Jesus was afraid to assert his power (139:12.2, 12.4); and Andrew sensing trouble in Judas without telling anyone (139:1.8). Judas’s hope that the raising of Lazarus meant a display of power draws on the apostles’ conclusion, after Lazarus, that Jesus might use his power in an emergency (171:3.4, 177:4.3).
ch15.b087: Added as fiction are the inner thoughts and memories of the apostles; the Philadelphia night and the Bethany garden; Thomas’s hands on the stone and his counting; Judas and Matthew going over the accounts; the brief remarks of Thomas and Philip; and the scene around the fire at Pella. The text says only that the apostles turned the children away, so John is placed among them. The apostle who said Lazarus would recover if he slept is not named in the text, and is not named here. Thomas’s speech keeps the sense of the text in new words.
ch15.b088: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
